metadata.title: Root separation for reducible integer polynomials

extraction_notes.note: Displayed equations are numbered by hand with plain-TeX \eqno inside $$...$$ and cited as bare "(n)" with no \label/\ref, so latex_facts reports none of them; I added the numbered displays by reading, and all their dependency edges are hand-made.

Numbered displays (2) and (6) are the bodies of later-cited inline claims and (10), (11) are cited prior results; each became a single claim/theorem node containing the display rather than a claim plus a separate equation node.
These end at a display closed by \eqno with no final period; the next sentence starts a new move, so the finishing step's mid-sentence warning is a false alarm.

The induction base sentence of claim (2) ("clearly true for d=0 and d=1") and the one-line divisibility justification ("easy to check") are flagged as immediate sentences, so I merged each with a neighbouring step. As a result claim (2)'s argument is two flat steps, not children of a claim step (step rules 6 and 7 conflict here).
L_n is introduced inside an outline remark and the O/<< convention is a notational stipulation; both are kept as definitions because later proofs rely on them.

Symbols introduced inside the proofs (p_{d,n}, x_n, y_{d,n}, q_{d,n}, K_n, s_{d,n}, r_{d,n}, F_k, R_{d,n}, Res_{d,n}) are proof steps, not definition nodes, per step rule 4; mentions of Wirsing's problem, Dujella-Pejkovic's e*(4)>=2 and Bombieri's Thue-Siegel principle are only referred to, so they get no nodes.

nodes.name: Naive height of an integer polynomial
nodes.statement:
The (na\"\i ve) height $H(P)$ of  an integer
polynomial $P(x)$ is
the maximum of the absolute values of its
coefficients.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.genus: the maximum of the absolute values of its coefficients

nodes.name: Root separation sep(P) and exponent e(P)
nodes.statement:
For a separable
integer polynomial $P(x)$ of degree $d \ge 2$
and with distinct roots $\alpha_1, \ldots , \alpha_d$,
we set
$$
{\rm sep}(P) = \min_{1 \le i < j \le d} \, |\alpha_i - \alpha_j|
$$
and define the quantity $e(P)$ by
$$
{\rm sep}(P) = H(P)^{-e(P)}.
$$
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement_short: sep(P) is the minimal distance between distinct roots of $P$; $e(P)$ is defined by sep$(P)=H(P)^{-e(P)}$.

nodes.name: Root separation exponents e(d) and e_irr(d)
nodes.statement:
Following the notation introduced in \cite{BM2}, for $d \ge 2$, we set
$$
e(d) := \limsup_{{\rm deg}(P) = d, H(P) \to + \infty} e(P)
$$
and
$$
e_{{\rm irr}} (d) := \limsup_{{\rm deg}(P) = d, H(P) \to + \infty} e(P),
$$
where the latter limsup is taken over the irreducible integer polynomials
$P(x)$ of degree $d$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement_short: $e(d)$ (resp. $e_{\rm irr}(d)$) is the limsup of $e(P)$ over integer (resp. irreducible) polynomials of degree $d$ as $H(P)\to\infty$.

nodes.name: Monic root separation exponents e*(d) and e*_irr(d)
nodes.statement:
We further define
$e^*(d)$ and $e_{{\rm irr}}^*(d)$ by restricting to
monic, respectively, monic irreducible integer polynomials, of degree $d$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Trivial comparison of separation exponents
nodes.statement:
Obviously, we have
$$
e(d) \ge e_{{\rm irr}}(d) \quad \mbox{and} \quad
e^*(d) \ge e_{{\rm irr}}^*(d), \quad (d \ge 2).
$$
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
conclusions:
e(d) \ge e_{{\rm irr}}(d) \quad \mbox{and} \quad
e^*(d) \ge e_{{\rm irr}}^*(d)

nodes.name: Mahler's root separation bound
nodes.statement:
A classical result of Mahler \cite{Mah64}
asserts that $e(d) \le d-1$ for every $d \ge 2$
and it is easy to check that $e_{{\rm irr}}(2)=e(2)=1$
and $e^*(2)=e_{{\rm irr}}^*(2) = 0$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement_short: Mahler: $e(d)\le d-1$ for all $d\ge 2$; also $e(2)=e_{\rm irr}(2)=1$ and $e^*(2)=e^*_{\rm irr}(2)=0$.

nodes.name: Evertse-Schonhage theorem on cubic root separation
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Previously known lower bounds for separation exponents
nodes.statement:
The following inequalities gather the lower bounds obtained
by Beresnevich, Bernik, Bugeaud, Dujella, G\"otze, and Mignotte in
the four papers \cite{BM1,BM2,BBG,BD}:
$$
e_{{\rm irr}}(d) \geq \frac{d}{2} +\frac{d-2}{4(d-1)}, \quad \mbox{for $d\geq 4$},
$$
$$
e (d)  \geq \frac{d+1}{2}, \quad \mbox{for odd $d\geq 5$},
$$
$$
e^*(3)=e_{{\rm irr}}^*(3) \geq \frac{3}{2}, \quad e^* (5) \ge 2,
\quad e_{{\rm irr}}^*(5) \ge \frac{7}{4},
$$
$$
e^*(d)\geq \frac{d}{2}, \quad e_{{\rm irr}}^*(d) \geq \frac{d-1}{2},
\quad \mbox{for even $d\geq 4$},
$$
and
$$
e^*(d)\geq \frac{d-1}{2}, \quad
e_{{\rm irr}}^*(d)\geq \frac{d}{2} +\frac{d-2}{4(d-1)} - 1, \quad \mbox{for odd $d\geq 7$}.
$$
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.origin_citation: Bugeaud & Mignotte 2004, 2010; Beresnevich, Bernik & Gotze 2010; Bugeaud & Dujella 2011
nodes.statement_short: Previously known lower bounds, all of order $d/2$, for $e(d)$, $e^*(d)$, $e_{\rm irr}(d)$, $e^*_{\rm irr}(d)$.

nodes.name: Lower bound for e(d)
nodes.statement:
For any integer $d\geq 4$, we have
$$
e(d)  \geq \frac{2d-1}{3}.
$$
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.label: tm1

nodes.name: Lower bound for e*(d) (monic polynomials)
nodes.statement:
For any even positive integer $d\geq 6$,  we have
$$
e^*(d) \geq \frac{2d-3}{3}.
$$
For any odd positive integer $d\geq 7$, we have
$$
e^*(d) \geq \frac{2d-5}{3}.
$$
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.label: tm2

nodes.name: Lower bounds of order 2d/3
nodes.statement:
Roughly speaking, all the previously known
lower bounds were of order $d/2$.
There are many other questions on integer polynomials of degree $d$,
or on algebraic numbers of degree $d$, for which the answer is known to lie
somewhere between $d/2$ and $d$. The most celebrated one is the problem
of Wirsing on the approximation to transcendental real numbers by algebraic
numbers of degree at most $d$; see Chapter 3 of \cite{BuLiv}.
We stress that the lower bounds in Theorems \ref{tm1} and \ref{tm2}
are of the order $2d/3$. As far as we are aware, this is the first time where
an estimate of order $\theta d$ with $\theta > 1/2$ is obtained for such kind of questions.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement_short: Previous bounds were of order $d/2$; Theorems 1 and 2 give order $2d/3$, the first $\theta d$ bound with $\theta>1/2$ for such questions.

nodes.name: Relation to Mahler's and Koksma's classifications
nodes.statement:
As pointed out in \cite{Bu1}, irreducible polynomials with close roots are useful
to investigate the difference between Mahler's and Koksma's classifications of real numbers.
However, it does not seem to us that Theorem \ref{tm1} could be applied to this question
to improve Corollary 1 of \cite{BD}.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Outline of the construction for Theorems 1 and 2
nodes.statement:
To prove Theorems 1 and 2 we construct parametric families
of integer polynomials. For an integer $d \ge 4$,
the reducible polynomials arising in the proof
of Theorem 1 are products of a linear polynomial
$L_n (x) = (n^2 + 3n +1)x - (n+2)$ with an irreducible
polynomial $p_{d-1, n} (x)$ of degree $d-1$ and height
of order $n$. We then show that $p_{d-1, n} (x)$ has a root
$y_{d,n}$ very close to the root $x_n = (n+2)/(n^2 + 3n + 1)$
of $L_n(x)$. Say differently, we construct a parametric family
$(y_{d,n})_{n \ge 1}$ of algebraic numbers of degree $d-1$ which are very
well approximated by a rational number with large height (in comparison to the
height of $y_{d,n}$). This means that it is then possible to apply Bombieri's version
of the Thue--Siegel principle \cite[Theorem 4]{Bom}
to the anchor pair $(y_{d,n}, x_n)$ to derive a rather good effective irrationality measure
for $y_{d,n}$ when $n$ is sufficiently large in comparison to $d$.
In his paper, Bombieri used the polynomials $x^d - n x  + 1$,
which have a root very close to the rational number $1/n$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement_short: Theorems 1-2 come from products of a linear polynomial $L_n$ with an irreducible $p_{d-1,n}$ having a root very close to the root $x_n$ of $L_n$.

nodes.name: Linear polynomial L_n
nodes.statement:
For an integer $d \ge 4$,
the reducible polynomials arising in the proof
of Theorem 1 are products of a linear polynomial
$L_n (x) = (n^2 + 3n +1)x - (n+2)$ with an irreducible
polynomial $p_{d-1, n} (x)$ of degree $d-1$ and height
of order $n$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Lower bound for e*_irr(d)
nodes.statement:
For any positive integer $d\geq 4$,  we have 
$$
e_{{\rm irr}}^* (d) \geq \frac{d}{2}-\frac{1}{4}.
$$
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.label: tm3

nodes.name: Convention on implied constants
nodes.statement:
Throughout the next sections, the constants implied by the symbols $O$, $\ll$ and
$\gg$ can be explicitly computed, are
independent of the parameter $n$, and depend at most on the degree $d$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1
nodes.statement:
We want to construct a one-parametric sequence of integer
polynomials $p_{d,n}(x)$ of degree $d$ having a root very close to the rational number
$x_n=(n+2)/(n^2+3n+1)$. Then the polynomials
$$
P_{d,n}(x)=((n^2+3n+1)x-(n+2)) p_{d-1,n}(x)
$$
will have two roots very close to each other.
We define the sequence $p_{d,n}(x)$ recursively by

$$
\eqalign{
& p_{0,n} (x) = -1, \quad p_{1,n} (x) = (n+1)x-1,  \cr
& p_{d,n} (x) = (1+x) p_{d-1,n}(x) +x^2 p_{d-2,n} (x). \cr} \eqno (1)
$$

We claim that

$$
p_{d,n}\left(\frac{n+2}{n^2+3n+1}\right) = \frac{(-1)^{d-1}}{(n^2+3n+1)^d}.    \eqno (2)
$$

Indeed, (2) is clearly true for $d=0$ and $d=1$. Assume now that $d \ge 1$
is an integer for which (2)
holds for $p_{d-1,n} (x)$ and $p_{d,n} (x)$.
Then we deduce from the recursion (1) that

$$
\eqalign{
p_{d,n}\left(\frac{n+2}{n^2+3n+1}\right)
& = \frac{(-1)^{d-2}}{(n^2+3n+1)^{d-1}} \cdot \frac{n^2+ 4n+3}{n^2+3n+1}  \cr
&   \, \, \, \, \, \, \, \, +
\frac{(-1)^{d-3}}{(n^2+3n+1)^{d-2}} \cdot \frac{n^2+ 4n+4}{(n^2+3n+1)^2} \cr
& = \frac{(-1)^{d-1}}{(n^2+3n+1)^d}, \cr}
$$

as claimed.

We now show that for sufficiently large $n$ the polynomial $p_{d,n} (x)$ has a root
between $x_n$ and
$$
z_{d,n}=x_n + \frac{(-1)^{d}}{n(n^2+3n+1)^d}.
$$
Observe that
$$
(-1)^{d-1} p_{d,n}(x_n) = \frac{1}{(n^2+3n+1)^d} > 0.
$$
By Rolle's theorem, there exists $z'_{d,n}$ between $x_n$ and $z_{d,n}$
such that
$$
p_{d,n}(z_{d,n})=p_{d,n}(x_n)+(z_{d,n}-x_n)p'_{d,n}(z'_{d,n}).
$$
It follows easily by induction that
$$
p_{d,n}(x)=-1+(n-d+2)x+((d-1)n-(d-1)(d-2)/2)x^2+\cdots
$$
Since $x_n=1/n+O(1/n^2)$, we have $p'_{d,n}(z'_{d,n}) = n + d + O(1/n)$.
Thus, for sufficiently large $n$, we get $p'_{d,n}(z'_{d,n}) > n$.
This implies that
$$
(-1)^{d-1}p_{d,n}(z_{d,n}) = \frac{1}{(n^2+3n+1)^d} - \frac{1}{n(n^2+3n+1)^d}p'_{d,n}(z'_{d,n}) < 0.
$$
Therefore, the polynomial $P_{d,n}(x)=((n^2+3n+1)x-(n+2)) p_{d-1,n}(x)$ has two close roots:
$x_n$ and $y_{d,n}$, which is between $x_n$ and $z_{d-1,n}$.
This yields
$$
{\rm sep}(P_{d,n}) \leq |x_n - y_{d,n} | \leq
\frac{1}{n(n^2+3n+1)^{d-1}} \leq \frac{1}{n^{2d-1}},   \eqno (3)
$$
when $n$ is large enough. Since the height of $P_{d,n} (x)$
is bounded from above by $n^3$ times a number depending only on $d$, this gives
$$
e(d)\geq \frac{2d-1}{3},
$$
by letting $n$ tend to infinity.
The proof of Theorem \ref{tm1} is complete.
\null \hfill \rule{2mm}{2mm}
nodes.section: 2 Reducible polynomials: Proof of Theorem 1
nodes.statement_short: Construct the recursive family $p_{d,n}$ whose value at $x_n=(n+2)/(n^2+3n+1)$ is tiny; a sign change gives a root of $p_{d-1,n}$ within $n^{-(2d-1)}$ of $x_n$, the root of $L_n$, with height $\ll n^3$.

nodes.name: Recursion defining p_{d,n}
nodes.section: 2 Reducible polynomials: Proof of Theorem 1

nodes.name: Value of p_{d,n} at x_n
nodes.statement:
We claim that

$$
p_{d,n}\left(\frac{n+2}{n^2+3n+1}\right) = \frac{(-1)^{d-1}}{(n^2+3n+1)^d}.    \eqno (2)
$$
nodes.section: 2 Reducible polynomials: Proof of Theorem 1

nodes.name: Separation bound for P_{d,n}
nodes.statement:
$$
{\rm sep}(P_{d,n}) \leq |x_n - y_{d,n} | \leq
\frac{1}{n(n^2+3n+1)^{d-1}} \leq \frac{1}{n^{2d-1}},   \eqno (3)
$$
nodes.section: 2 Reducible polynomials: Proof of Theorem 1

nodes.name: Irreducibility of p_{d-1,n}
nodes.statement:
By Gelfond's inequality (see e.g.  \cite[Lemma A.3]{BuLiv}),
the height of $y_{d,n}$ is $\ll  n$.
Liouville's inequality (see e.g.  \cite[Theorem A.1]{BuLiv}) then implies that
$$
|x_n - y_{d,n}| \gg  n^{-2 \delta-1},
$$
where $\delta$ denotes the degree of $y_{d,n}$.
Combined with (3), this gives $\delta = d-1$ and establishes that
the polynomial $p_{d-1,n} (x)$ must be irreducible.
nodes.section: 2 Reducible polynomials: Proof of Theorem 1
nodes.statement_short: Gelfond and Liouville inequalities combined with (3) force $y_{d,n}$ to have degree $d-1$, so $p_{d-1,n}$ is irreducible.

nodes.name: Sharpness of Liouville's inequality
nodes.statement:
Also, (3) shows that Liouville's inequality
$$
|x_n - y_{d,n}| \gg  n^{-2d+1}
$$
is sharp in terms of $n$.
nodes.section: 2 Reducible polynomials: Proof of Theorem 1

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement:
In order to get a family of monic polynomials with similar
separation properties as the family $P_{d,n}(x)$, we replace the
linear non-monic polynomial $L_n(x)=(n^2+3n+1)x-(n+2)$ by
the monic quadratic polynomial
$$
K_n(x)=x^2 - (n^2+3n+1)x+(n+2).
$$
Thus, we want to construct a one-parametric sequence of integer
polynomials $q_{d,n}(x)$ of degree $d$ having a root very close
to the root $y_n=1/n+O(1/n^2)$ of $K_n(x)$.
Then the polynomials
$$
Q_{d,n}(x)=(x^2 - (n^2+3n+1)x+(n+2)) q_{d-2,n}(x)
$$
will have two roots very close to each other.

For $d \ge 0$ even, we define the sequence $q_{d,n}(x)$ recursively by
$$
\eqalign{
& q_{0,n} (x) = 1, \quad q_{2,n} (x) = x^2-(n+1)x+1, \cr
& q_{d,n} (x) = (2x^2 + x + 1) q_{d-2,n} (x) -  x^4 q_{d-4,n} (x). \cr} \eqno (4)
$$
We claim that $q_{d,n} (x)- q_{d-2,n} (x) q_{2,n} (x)$ is divisible by $K_n (x)$.
This is easy to check for $d=2$ and $d=4$,
and then the claim follows by induction using the recursion (4).
This yields that
$$
q_{d,n}(y_n) = q_{d-2,n}(y_n)q_{2,n}(y_n) = (q_{2,n}(y_n))^{d/2},
$$
for $d \ge 2$ even. From
$$
y_n=1/n-1/n^2+2/n^3-4/n^4+8/n^5+ O(1/n^6),
$$
we get $q_{2,n}(y_n)=1/n^4 + O(1/n^5)$ and hence
$$
q_{d,n}(y_n) = 1/n^{2d} + O(1/n^{2d+1}).
$$


We now show that for sufficiently large $n$ the polynomial $q_{d,n} (x)$ has a root
between $y_n$ and $w_{d,n}=y_n + \frac{2}{n^{2d+1}}$.
We have
$$
q_{d,n}(y_n) = 1/n^{2d} + O(1/n^{2d+1}) > 0.
$$
By Rolle's theorem, there exists $w'_{d,n}$ between $y_n$ and $w_{d,n}$ such that
$$
q_{d,n}(w_{d,n})=q_{d,n}(y_n)+(w_{d,n}-y_n)q'_{d,n}(w'_{d,n}).
$$
It follows easily by induction that
$$
q_{d,n}(x)=1+(-n+d/2-2)x+((-d/2+1)n+(d^2-2d+8)/8)x^2+\cdots
$$
Since $y_n=1/n+O(1/n^2)$, we have $q'_{d,n}(w'_{d,n}) = -n - d/2 + O(1/n)$.
Thus, for sufficiently large $n$, we get $q'_{d,n}(w'_{d,n}) < -n$.
This implies
$$
q_{d,n}(w_{d,n}) = 1/n^{2d} + O(1/n^{2d+1}) + \frac{2}{n^{2d+1}}q'_{d,n}(w'_{d,n}) < 0.
$$

Thus, the polynomial $Q_{d,n}(x)=(x^2 - (n^2+3n+1)x+(n+2)) q_{d-2,n}(x)$
has two close roots:
$y_n$ and $v_{d,n}$, which is between $y_n$ and $w_{d-2,n}$.
This yields
$$
{\rm sep}(Q_{d,n}) \leq \frac{2}{n^{2d-3}},
$$
when $n$ is large enough.
Since $H(Q_{d,n})=O(n^3)$, this gives
$$
e^*(d)\geq \frac{2d-3}{3},
$$
by letting $n$ tend to infinity.

Let now $d$ be odd. Then we define
$$ Q_{d,n}(x)=x(x^2 - (n^2+3n+1)x+(n+2)) q_{d-3,n}(x). $$
This polynomial has two close roots:
$y_n$ and a root lying between $y_n$ and $w_{d-3,n}$.
Thus we get
$$
{\rm sep}(Q_{d,n}) \leq \frac{2}{n^{2d-5}},
$$
for $n$ large enough, and
$$
e^*(d)\geq \frac{2d-5}{3}.
$$
The proof of Theorem \ref{tm2} is complete.
\null \hfill \rule{2mm}{2mm}
nodes.section: 3 Reducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement_short: Replace $L_n$ by the monic quadratic $K_n$ and build a recursive family $q_{d,n}$ with a root near the root $y_n$ of $K_n$; height $O(n^3)$, separation $\ll n^{-(2d-3)}$. Odd $d$ uses an extra factor $x$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement:
In this section, we use the polynomials $p_{d,n}(x)$
to construct irreducible monic polynomials
having two very close roots.
Let $F_k$ denote the $k$th Fibonacci number defined by
the recursion $F_0=0$, $F_1=1$ and $F_k=F_{k-1}+F_{k-2}$ for $k \ge 2$.
Note that Fibonacci numbers appear in the asymptotic expansion of
$x_n = (n+2) / (n^2 + 3n + 1)$, namely
$$
x_n = 1/n-1/n^2+2/n^3-5/n^4+13/n^5-34/n^6+ \cdots - (-1)^k F_{2k-3}/n^{k} + \cdots
$$
For $d\geq 0$, we first define
monic polynomials $s_{d,n}(x)$ with a root close to $x_n $ by
$$
s_{d,n} (x)=(-1)^{d-1}(F_{d-1}p_{d,n}(x) - F_d x p_{d-1,n} (x)),
$$
and then monic polynomials with two close roots by
$$
\eqalign{
r_{2d+1,n} (x) & = xs_{d,n}^2(x) + F_d^2 p_{d,n}^2 (x),  \cr
r_{2d,n}(x) & = s_{d,n}^2 (x) + F_{d-1}^2 x p_{d-1,n}^2 (x). \cr} \eqno (5)
$$
We claim that these polynomials are monic.
It suffices to show that this is true for $s_{d,n}(x)$.
Since the leading coefficient of $p_{d,n} (x)$ is $F_d n + F_{d-2}$,
we deduce that the leading coefficient of $s_{d,n}(x)$ is equal to
\begin{eqnarray*}
& (-1)^{d-1} (F_{d-1}(F_d n + F_{d-2})-F_d(F_{d-1}n + F_{d-3})) \\ 
& =
(-1)^{d-1}(F_{d-1}F_{d-2}-F_dF_{d-3}) = 1.
\end{eqnarray*}

From (2) we get
$$
r_{2d+1,n}(x_n )=F_d^2/n^{4d-1} + O(1/n^{4d})
$$
and
$$
r_{2d,n}(x_n )=F_{d-1}^2/n^{4d-3} + O(1/n^{4d-2}),
$$
that is,
$$
r_{d,n}(x_n )=F_{\lfloor (d-1)/2 \rfloor}^2/n^{2d-3} + O(1/n^{2d-2}).
$$

Observe that the degree of the polynomial $r_{d,n} (x)$ is $d$. 
We claim that
$r_{d,n} (x)$ has two complex conjugate roots $v_{d,n}$ and
$\overline{v_{d,n}}$ close to $x_n $,
more precisely they are equal to
$$
\eqalign{
1/n-1/n^2+2/n^3- & 5/n^4+13/n^5- \ldots + \cr
& + (-1)^d F_{2d-5}/n^{d-1} \pm i/n^{(2d-1)/2} + O(1/n^{d}). \cr} \eqno (6)
$$
Indeed, the polynomials $F_d^2 p_{d,n}^2(x)$ and $F_{d-1}^2 x p_{d-1,n}^2(x)$
have double 
roots $y_{d+1,n}$ and $y_{d,n}$, resp., in the disc 
$|x-x_n|\leq 1/n^{2d+1}$,
resp. $|x-x_n|\leq 1/n^{2d-1}$.
Moreover, we have $F_d^2 p_{d,n}^2(x) < xs_{d,n}^2(x)$ when 
$|x-x_n| = 1/n^{2d+1}$
and $F_{d-1}^2 x p_{d-1,n}^2(x) < s_{d,n}^2(x)$ when 
$|x-x_n| = 1/n^{2d-1}$.
Hence, by Rouch\'e's theorem, the polynomial
$r_{d,n} (x)$ has two roots $v$ satisfying $|v-x_n |<1/n^{d-1}$.
Using a complex version of Taylor's theorem,
by writing the roots $v$ of $r_{d,n} (x)$ close to $x_n$
as $v =x_n +\beta+\gamma i$ with $\gamma > 0$, we get 
$$
\eqalign{
0 & =r_{d,n}(x_n +\beta+\gamma i) \cr
& = r_{d,n}(x_n ) + (\beta+\gamma i)r'_{d,n}(x_n )+
(\beta+\gamma i)^2r''_{d,n}(x_n )/2+ O(1/n^{3d-5}). \cr}
$$
Note that we have
$$
r'_{2d+1,n}(x_n ) =\frac{2F_dF_{d+1}}{n^{2d-1}} + O(1/n^{2d}),
$$
$$
r'_{2d,n}(x_n ) =\frac{2F_{d-1}F_{d-2}}{n^{2d-2}} + O(1/n^{2d-1}),
$$
and
$$
r''_{d,n}(x_n ) = 2F_{\lfloor (d-1)/2 \rfloor}^2 n^2 + O(n).
$$
By considering imaginary parts in the above Taylor's formula we get
\begin{eqnarray*}
\beta &=& - \frac{r'_{d,n}(x_n)}{r''_{d,n}(x_n)} + O(\gamma^{-1}r''_{d,n}(x_n)^{-1}n^{-3d+5}) \\
 &=& - \frac{F_{\lfloor (d-1)/2 \rfloor + (-1)^d}}{n^d} + O\left(\frac{1}{n^{d+1}}\right) +
O\left(\frac{1}{\gamma n^{3d-3}}\right).
\end{eqnarray*}
Since the distance between the roots $x_n +\beta+\gamma i$ and  
$x_n +\beta-\gamma i$ of $r_{d,n} (x)$ is equal to $2 \gamma$  
and $H(r_{d,n})=O(n^2)$, 
it follows from Mahler's theorem \cite{Mah64} quoted in the introduction that 
$\gamma \gg 1/n^{2d-2}$. Thus, $\beta = O(1/n^{d-1})$.
Moreover, $\beta = O(1/n^d)$, unless $\gamma \ll 1/n^{2d-3}$.
Looking at real parts leads to
$$
\eqalign{
\frac{F_{\lfloor (d-1)/2 \rfloor}^2}{n^{2d-3}} +
\frac{2\beta F_{\lfloor (d-1)/2 \rfloor}F_{\lfloor (d-1)/2 \rfloor
+ (-1)^d}}{n^{d-2}} + (\beta^2 - \gamma^2) &
F_{\lfloor (d-1)/2 \rfloor}^2 n^2 \cr
& = O\left(\frac{1}{n^{2d-2}}\right).}  \eqno{(7)}
$$
The assumption that $\gamma \ll 1/n^{2d-3}$ leads to a contradiction, 
by considering (7) as a quadratic equation
in $\beta$. Hence, we have $\beta = O(1/n^{d})$. Now (7) gives
$\gamma^2 = 1/n^{2d-1} + O(1/n^{2d})$, i.e.,
$\gamma = 1/n^{(2d-1)/2} + O(1/n^d)$, as claimed in (6). 

Let $R_{d,n}(x)$ be the irreducible factor of $r_{d,n}(x)$ having roots
$v_{d,n}$ and $\overline{v_{d,n}}$. Denote by $\delta$ its degree.
Note that, since $H(r_{d,n})=O(n^2)$, Gelfond's inequality implies that
$$
H(R_{d,n})=O(n^2).    \eqno (8)
$$

Denote by ${\rm Res}_{d,n}$ the resultant of
the polynomials $R_{d,n} (x)$ and $L_n(x)$.
Since ${\rm Res}_{d,n}$ is a rational integer and $x_n$ is not a root of $R_{d,n} (x)$, we have
$$
|{\rm Res}_{d,n}| \ge 1.   \eqno (9)
$$
Furthermore, the definition of the resultant of two polynomials (see e.g. \cite[p. 223]{BuLiv})
implies that (recall that $R_{d,n}(x)$ is monic)
$$
|{\rm Res}_{d,n}| \le  (n^2 + 3n+1)^{\delta} \prod_{t : R_{d,n} (t) = 0} \, |t - x_n|.
$$
Since the product of the absolute values of all the roots of $R_{d,n} (x)$
different from $v_{d,n}$ and $\overline{v_{d,n}}$ is bounded
from above by $\sqrt{d+1}$ times
the height of $R_{d,n} (x)$ (see \cite[Exercise A.1]{BuLiv}), we deduce from (6) and (8) that
$$
|{\rm Res}_{d,n}| \ll n^{2 \delta} n^{-2d+1} n^2.
$$
Combined with (9), this gives $2 \delta \ge 2d - 3$, thus
$$
\delta \in  \{d, d-1\}.
$$
This implies that either $r_{d,n}(x)$ is irreducible, or it has an integer
root (recall that any rational root of a monic polynomial must be a rational
integer).

Assume that $r_{d,n}(x)$ is reducible, i.e., that it has an integer root.
This integer must divide $r_{d,n}(0)=F_{\lfloor (d-1)/2 \rfloor}^2$,
and, by (5),
it is of the form $-\alpha^2$ for an integer $\alpha$ dividing $F_{\lfloor (d-1)/2 \rfloor}$.
So, for any given degree $d$, there are only finitely many possibilities for the integer root
of $r_{d,n}(x)$.

Write $r_{d,n}(x)$ as
$$
r_{d,n}(x)=A_d(x)n^2+B_d(x)n+C_d(x).
$$
By the definition of $r_{d,n}(x)$ and (1), it follows easily by induction
that the discriminant $B_d(x)^2 - 4A_d(x)C_d(x)$ of $r_{d,n}(x)$ with respect to $n$
is equal to $-4 F_{\lfloor (d-1)/2 \rfloor}^4 x^{2d-1}$.
In particular, this discriminant is nonzero at $x=-\alpha^2$,
and thus at least one of the numbers $A_d(-\alpha^2)$, $B_d(-\alpha^2)$, $C_d(-\alpha^2)$
is nonzero.
This shows that $r_{d,n}(x)$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Z}[n,x]$.

Furthermore, for given $\alpha$ there are exactly two (rational) values of $n$
such that $-\alpha^2$ is a root of $r_{d,n}(x)$. Hence, for sufficiently large
positive integer $n$, the polynomial $r_{d,n}(x)$ has no integer roots,
and therefore it is irreducible over $\mathbb{Z}[x]$.

Since
$$
{\rm sep}(r_{d,n}) = O(n^{-(d-1/2)}),
$$
we obtain
$$
e_{{\rm irr}}^* (d) \geq \frac{2d-1}{4},
$$
which proves Theorem \ref{tm3}.
\null \hfill \rule{2mm}{2mm}

nodes.name: Mahler's inequality for products of root distances
nodes.statement:
Let $d \ge 2$ be an integer.
Mahler's upper bound $e(d) \le d-1$ quoted in the Introduction
is a particular case of the lower bound
$$
\prod_{1\le i<j\le k} \vert \alpha_i -\alpha_j \vert  \gg  H(P)^{- d +1},
\eqno (10)
$$
valid for any integer polynomial $P(x)$ of degree $d$ having
at least $k \ge 2$
distinct roots $\alpha_1, \ldots , \alpha_k$, established in \cite{Mah64}.
nodes.section: 5 Clusters of roots
assumptions:
any integer polynomial $P(x)$ of degree $d$ having
at least $k \ge 2$
distinct roots $\alpha_1, \ldots , \alpha_k$
nodes.statement_short: Mahler: for $k\ge2$ distinct roots of an integer polynomial of degree $d$, the product of their pairwise distances is $\gg H(P)^{-d+1}$.

nodes.name: Cluster separation exponents E(d,k) and E_irr(d,k)
nodes.statement:
Let $k$ and $d$ be integers with $2 \le k \le d$.
We denote by $E(d,k)$, respectively
$E_{{\rm irr}}(d,k)$, the infimum of the real numbers $\delta$
for which
$$
\prod_{1\le i<j\le k} \vert \alpha_i -\alpha_j \vert  \ge H(P)^{- \delta}
$$
holds for every integer polynomial $P(x)$, respectively,
irreducible integer polynomial $P(x)$,
of degree $d$ and sufficiently large
height, with distinct roots $\alpha_1, \ldots , \alpha_d$.
nodes.section: 5 Clusters of roots
nodes.genus: the infimum of the real numbers $\delta$
nodes.statement_short: $E(d,k)$ is the infimum of $\delta$ with $\prod_{i<j\le k}|\alpha_i-\alpha_j|\ge H(P)^{-\delta}$ for all (irreducible) integer $P$ of degree $d$ and large height.

nodes.name: Bugeaud-Mignotte lower bounds for clusters
nodes.statement:

it is proved in \cite{BM1,BM2} that, for any integer $d \ge 4$
and any integer $k\ge 2$ that divides $d$, we have
$$
E(d, k) \ge \frac{k-1}{k} d  \quad \mbox{and} \quad
E^* (d, k) \ge \frac{k-1}{k} d - \frac{k-1}{2}.  \eqno (11)
$$

$$

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4
nodes.statement:
Let $\delta \ge 2$ and $h \ge 0$ be integers. The polynomial
$$
{\tilde P}_{\delta, h, n} (x) :=
P_{\delta, n} (x) \times p_{\delta,n} (x) \times \cdots \times p_{\delta+h, n} (x)
$$
has degree $(h+2)\delta + h(h+1)/2$, height $\ll  n^{h+4}$, and
it has a cluster of $h+3$ roots close
to each other. Setting $k = h+3$, a short calculation gives (12), since one can
multiply ${\tilde P}_{\delta, h, n} (x)$ by a suitable power of the monomial $x$.
To get (13), it suffices, for $\delta$ even, to consider the polynomial
$$
{\tilde Q}_{\delta, h, n} (x) :=
Q_{\delta, n} (x) \times q_{\delta,n} (x) \times \cdots \times q_{\delta + 2 h, n} (x),
$$
multiplied by a suitable power of the monomial $x$.
We omit the details.

nodes.statement_short: Multiply $P_{\delta,n}$ by consecutive $p_{\delta+j,n}$ (resp. $Q$ by $q$'s) to get a cluster of $h+3$ close roots with controlled height; details omitted.

nodes.name: Goal of the construction
nodes.statement:
We want to construct a one-parametric sequence of integer
polynomials $p_{d,n}(x)$ of degree $d$ having a root very close to the rational number
$x_n=(n+2)/(n^2+3n+1)$. Then the polynomials
$$
P_{d,n}(x)=((n^2+3n+1)x-(n+2)) p_{d-1,n}(x)
$$
will have two roots very close to each other.
nodes.section: 2 Reducible polynomials: Proof of Theorem 1
nodes.statement_short: Aim: polynomials $p_{d,n}$ with a root near $x_n$, so $P_{d,n}=L_n p_{d-1,n}$ has two close roots.

nodes.name: Define p_{d,n} recursively
nodes.statement:
We define the sequence $p_{d,n}(x)$ recursively by

$$
\eqalign{
& p_{0,n} (x) = -1, \quad p_{1,n} (x) = (n+1)x-1,  \cr
& p_{d,n} (x) = (1+x) p_{d-1,n}(x) +x^2 p_{d-2,n} (x). \cr} \eqno (1)
$$
nodes.section: 2 Reducible polynomials: Proof of Theorem 1
nodes.statement_short: Define $p_{d,n}$ by the three-term recursion (1).

nodes.name: Claim (2): statement, base cases, hypothesis
nodes.statement:
We claim that

$$
p_{d,n}\left(\frac{n+2}{n^2+3n+1}\right) = \frac{(-1)^{d-1}}{(n^2+3n+1)^d}.    \eqno (2)
$$

Indeed, (2) is clearly true for $d=0$ and $d=1$. Assume now that $d \ge 1$
is an integer for which (2)
holds for $p_{d-1,n} (x)$ and $p_{d,n} (x)$.
nodes.section: 2 Reducible polynomials: Proof of Theorem 1
nodes.statement_short: Claim $p_{d,n}(x_n)=(-1)^{d-1}/(n^2+3n+1)^d$; base cases $d=0,1$ and induction hypothesis.

nodes.name: Inductive step
nodes.statement:
Then we deduce from the recursion (1) that

$$
\eqalign{
p_{d,n}\left(\frac{n+2}{n^2+3n+1}\right)
& = \frac{(-1)^{d-2}}{(n^2+3n+1)^{d-1}} \cdot \frac{n^2+ 4n+3}{n^2+3n+1}  \cr
&   \, \, \, \, \, \, \, \, +
\frac{(-1)^{d-3}}{(n^2+3n+1)^{d-2}} \cdot \frac{n^2+ 4n+4}{(n^2+3n+1)^2} \cr
& = \frac{(-1)^{d-1}}{(n^2+3n+1)^d}, \cr}
$$

as claimed.
nodes.section: 2 Reducible polynomials: Proof of Theorem 1
nodes.statement_short: Inductive step via recursion (1) completes claim (2).

nodes.name: Root of p_{d,n} near x_n
nodes.statement:
We now show that for sufficiently large $n$ the polynomial $p_{d,n} (x)$ has a root
between $x_n$ and
$$
z_{d,n}=x_n + \frac{(-1)^{d}}{n(n^2+3n+1)^d}.
$$
Observe that
$$
(-1)^{d-1} p_{d,n}(x_n) = \frac{1}{(n^2+3n+1)^d} > 0.
$$
By Rolle's theorem, there exists $z'_{d,n}$ between $x_n$ and $z_{d,n}$
such that
$$
p_{d,n}(z_{d,n})=p_{d,n}(x_n)+(z_{d,n}-x_n)p'_{d,n}(z'_{d,n}).
$$
It follows easily by induction that
$$
p_{d,n}(x)=-1+(n-d+2)x+((d-1)n-(d-1)(d-2)/2)x^2+\cdots
$$
Since $x_n=1/n+O(1/n^2)$, we have $p'_{d,n}(z'_{d,n}) = n + d + O(1/n)$.
Thus, for sufficiently large $n$, we get $p'_{d,n}(z'_{d,n}) > n$.
This implies that
$$
(-1)^{d-1}p_{d,n}(z_{d,n}) = \frac{1}{(n^2+3n+1)^d} - \frac{1}{n(n^2+3n+1)^d}p'_{d,n}(z'_{d,n}) < 0.
$$
nodes.section: 2 Reducible polynomials: Proof of Theorem 1
nodes.statement_short: Show $p_{d,n}$ has a root between $x_n$ and $z_{d,n}$ by a sign change.

nodes.name: Sign at x_n
nodes.section: 2 Reducible polynomials: Proof of Theorem 1

nodes.name: Mean value step
nodes.statement:
By Rolle's theorem, there exists $z'_{d,n}$ between $x_n$ and $z_{d,n}$
such that
$$
p_{d,n}(z_{d,n})=p_{d,n}(x_n)+(z_{d,n}-x_n)p'_{d,n}(z'_{d,n}).
$$
nodes.section: 2 Reducible polynomials: Proof of Theorem 1
nodes.statement_short: Mean value expansion between $x_n$ and $z_{d,n}$.

nodes.name: Low-order coefficients
nodes.statement:
It follows easily by induction that
$$
p_{d,n}(x)=-1+(n-d+2)x+((d-1)n-(d-1)(d-2)/2)x^2+\cdots
$$
nodes.section: 2 Reducible polynomials: Proof of Theorem 1
nodes.statement_short: First coefficients of $p_{d,n}$ by induction.

nodes.name: Derivative estimate
nodes.statement:
Since $x_n=1/n+O(1/n^2)$, we have $p'_{d,n}(z'_{d,n}) = n + d + O(1/n)$.
Thus, for sufficiently large $n$, we get $p'_{d,n}(z'_{d,n}) > n$.
nodes.section: 2 Reducible polynomials: Proof of Theorem 1
nodes.statement_short: $p'_{d,n}(z'_{d,n})>n$ for large $n$.

nodes.name: Sign at z_{d,n}
nodes.section: 2 Reducible polynomials: Proof of Theorem 1
nodes.statement_short: Sign change, so a root lies between $x_n$ and $z_{d,n}$.

nodes.name: Separation of P_{d,n}
nodes.statement:
Therefore, the polynomial $P_{d,n}(x)=((n^2+3n+1)x-(n+2)) p_{d-1,n}(x)$ has two close roots:
$x_n$ and $y_{d,n}$, which is between $x_n$ and $z_{d-1,n}$.
This yields
$$
{\rm sep}(P_{d,n}) \leq |x_n - y_{d,n} | \leq
\frac{1}{n(n^2+3n+1)^{d-1}} \leq \frac{1}{n^{2d-1}},   \eqno (3)
$$
when $n$ is large enough.
nodes.section: 2 Reducible polynomials: Proof of Theorem 1
nodes.statement_short: sep$(P_{d,n})\le n^{-(2d-1)}$, giving (3).

nodes.name: Conclude Theorem 1
nodes.statement:
Since the height of $P_{d,n} (x)$
is bounded from above by $n^3$ times a number depending only on $d$, this gives
$$
e(d)\geq \frac{2d-1}{3},
$$
by letting $n$ tend to infinity.
The proof of Theorem \ref{tm1} is complete.
\null \hfill \rule{2mm}{2mm}
nodes.section: 2 Reducible polynomials: Proof of Theorem 1
nodes.statement_short: Height $\ll n^3$ gives $e(d)\ge(2d-1)/3$.

nodes.name: Monic quadratic K_n and target family
nodes.statement:
In order to get a family of monic polynomials with similar
separation properties as the family $P_{d,n}(x)$, we replace the
linear non-monic polynomial $L_n(x)=(n^2+3n+1)x-(n+2)$ by
the monic quadratic polynomial
$$
K_n(x)=x^2 - (n^2+3n+1)x+(n+2).
$$
Thus, we want to construct a one-parametric sequence of integer
polynomials $q_{d,n}(x)$ of degree $d$ having a root very close
to the root $y_n=1/n+O(1/n^2)$ of $K_n(x)$.
Then the polynomials
$$
Q_{d,n}(x)=(x^2 - (n^2+3n+1)x+(n+2)) q_{d-2,n}(x)
$$
will have two roots very close to each other.
nodes.section: 3 Reducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement_short: Replace $L_n$ by monic $K_n$; seek $q_{d,n}$ with a root near the root $y_n$ of $K_n$.

nodes.name: Define q_{d,n} recursively
nodes.statement:
For $d \ge 0$ even, we define the sequence $q_{d,n}(x)$ recursively by
$$
\eqalign{
& q_{0,n} (x) = 1, \quad q_{2,n} (x) = x^2-(n+1)x+1, \cr
& q_{d,n} (x) = (2x^2 + x + 1) q_{d-2,n} (x) -  x^4 q_{d-4,n} (x). \cr} \eqno (4)
$$
nodes.section: 3 Reducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement_short: Define $q_{d,n}$ by recursion (4).

nodes.name: Divisibility by K_n and value at y_n
nodes.statement:
We claim that $q_{d,n} (x)- q_{d-2,n} (x) q_{2,n} (x)$ is divisible by $K_n (x)$.
This is easy to check for $d=2$ and $d=4$,
and then the claim follows by induction using the recursion (4).
This yields that
$$
q_{d,n}(y_n) = q_{d-2,n}(y_n)q_{2,n}(y_n) = (q_{2,n}(y_n))^{d/2},
$$
for $d \ge 2$ even.
nodes.section: 3 Reducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement_short: $K_n$ divides $q_{d,n}-q_{d-2,n}q_{2,n}$ (induction), so $q_{d,n}(y_n)=q_{2,n}(y_n)^{d/2}$.

nodes.name: Asymptotics of q_{d,n}(y_n)
nodes.section: 3 Reducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 2

nodes.name: Root of q_{d,n} near y_n
nodes.statement:
We now show that for sufficiently large $n$ the polynomial $q_{d,n} (x)$ has a root
between $y_n$ and $w_{d,n}=y_n + \frac{2}{n^{2d+1}}$.
We have
$$
q_{d,n}(y_n) = 1/n^{2d} + O(1/n^{2d+1}) > 0.
$$
By Rolle's theorem, there exists $w'_{d,n}$ between $y_n$ and $w_{d,n}$ such that
$$
q_{d,n}(w_{d,n})=q_{d,n}(y_n)+(w_{d,n}-y_n)q'_{d,n}(w'_{d,n}).
$$
It follows easily by induction that
$$
q_{d,n}(x)=1+(-n+d/2-2)x+((-d/2+1)n+(d^2-2d+8)/8)x^2+\cdots
$$
Since $y_n=1/n+O(1/n^2)$, we have $q'_{d,n}(w'_{d,n}) = -n - d/2 + O(1/n)$.
Thus, for sufficiently large $n$, we get $q'_{d,n}(w'_{d,n}) < -n$.
This implies
$$
q_{d,n}(w_{d,n}) = 1/n^{2d} + O(1/n^{2d+1}) + \frac{2}{n^{2d+1}}q'_{d,n}(w'_{d,n}) < 0.
$$
nodes.section: 3 Reducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement_short: Sign change shows a root between $y_n$ and $w_{d,n}$.

nodes.name: Sign at y_n
nodes.section: 3 Reducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 2

nodes.name: Mean value step
nodes.statement:
By Rolle's theorem, there exists $w'_{d,n}$ between $y_n$ and $w_{d,n}$ such that
$$
q_{d,n}(w_{d,n})=q_{d,n}(y_n)+(w_{d,n}-y_n)q'_{d,n}(w'_{d,n}).
$$
nodes.section: 3 Reducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement_short: Mean value expansion between $y_n$ and $w_{d,n}$.

nodes.name: Low-order coefficients
nodes.statement:
It follows easily by induction that
$$
q_{d,n}(x)=1+(-n+d/2-2)x+((-d/2+1)n+(d^2-2d+8)/8)x^2+\cdots
$$
nodes.section: 3 Reducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement_short: First coefficients of $q_{d,n}$ by induction.

nodes.name: Derivative estimate
nodes.statement:
Since $y_n=1/n+O(1/n^2)$, we have $q'_{d,n}(w'_{d,n}) = -n - d/2 + O(1/n)$.
Thus, for sufficiently large $n$, we get $q'_{d,n}(w'_{d,n}) < -n$.
nodes.section: 3 Reducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement_short: $q'_{d,n}(w'_{d,n})<-n$ for large $n$.

nodes.name: Sign at w_{d,n}
nodes.section: 3 Reducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement_short: Sign change.

nodes.name: Separation of Q_{d,n}
nodes.statement:
Thus, the polynomial $Q_{d,n}(x)=(x^2 - (n^2+3n+1)x+(n+2)) q_{d-2,n}(x)$
has two close roots:
$y_n$ and $v_{d,n}$, which is between $y_n$ and $w_{d-2,n}$.
This yields
$$
{\rm sep}(Q_{d,n}) \leq \frac{2}{n^{2d-3}},
$$
when $n$ is large enough.
nodes.section: 3 Reducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement_short: sep$(Q_{d,n})\le 2n^{-(2d-3)}$ for even $d$.

nodes.name: Conclude even case
nodes.statement:
Since $H(Q_{d,n})=O(n^3)$, this gives
$$
e^*(d)\geq \frac{2d-3}{3},
$$
by letting $n$ tend to infinity.
nodes.section: 3 Reducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement_short: Height $O(n^3)$ gives $e^*(d)\ge(2d-3)/3$ for even $d$.

nodes.name: Odd degree case
nodes.statement:
Let now $d$ be odd. Then we define
$$ Q_{d,n}(x)=x(x^2 - (n^2+3n+1)x+(n+2)) q_{d-3,n}(x). $$
This polynomial has two close roots:
$y_n$ and a root lying between $y_n$ and $w_{d-3,n}$.
Thus we get
$$
{\rm sep}(Q_{d,n}) \leq \frac{2}{n^{2d-5}},
$$
for $n$ large enough, and
$$
e^*(d)\geq \frac{2d-5}{3}.
$$
The proof of Theorem \ref{tm2} is complete.
\null \hfill \rule{2mm}{2mm}
nodes.section: 3 Reducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement_short: Odd $d$: multiply by $x$ and use $q_{d-3,n}$, giving $e^*(d)\ge(2d-5)/3$.

nodes.name: Plan
nodes.statement:
In this section, we use the polynomials $p_{d,n}(x)$
to construct irreducible monic polynomials
having two very close roots.
nodes.section: 4 Irreducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement_short: Use $p_{d,n}$ to build irreducible monic polynomials with two close roots.

nodes.name: Fibonacci numbers and expansion of x_n
nodes.statement:
Let $F_k$ denote the $k$th Fibonacci number defined by
the recursion $F_0=0$, $F_1=1$ and $F_k=F_{k-1}+F_{k-2}$ for $k \ge 2$.
Note that Fibonacci numbers appear in the asymptotic expansion of
$x_n = (n+2) / (n^2 + 3n + 1)$, namely
$$
x_n = 1/n-1/n^2+2/n^3-5/n^4+13/n^5-34/n^6+ \cdots - (-1)^k F_{2k-3}/n^{k} + \cdots
$$
nodes.section: 4 Irreducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement_short: Introduce Fibonacci numbers, which appear in the expansion of $x_n$.

nodes.name: Define s_{d,n} and r_{d,n}
nodes.statement:
For $d\geq 0$, we first define
monic polynomials $s_{d,n}(x)$ with a root close to $x_n $ by
$$
s_{d,n} (x)=(-1)^{d-1}(F_{d-1}p_{d,n}(x) - F_d x p_{d-1,n} (x)),
$$
and then monic polynomials with two close roots by
$$
\eqalign{
r_{2d+1,n} (x) & = xs_{d,n}^2(x) + F_d^2 p_{d,n}^2 (x),  \cr
r_{2d,n}(x) & = s_{d,n}^2 (x) + F_{d-1}^2 x p_{d-1,n}^2 (x). \cr} \eqno (5)
$$
nodes.section: 4 Irreducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement_short: Define monic $s_{d,n}$ and $r_{d,n}$ via (5).

nodes.name: Monicity of r_{d,n}
nodes.statement:
We claim that these polynomials are monic.
It suffices to show that this is true for $s_{d,n}(x)$.
Since the leading coefficient of $p_{d,n} (x)$ is $F_d n + F_{d-2}$,
we deduce that the leading coefficient of $s_{d,n}(x)$ is equal to
\begin{eqnarray*}
& (-1)^{d-1} (F_{d-1}(F_d n + F_{d-2})-F_d(F_{d-1}n + F_{d-3})) \\ 
& =
(-1)^{d-1}(F_{d-1}F_{d-2}-F_dF_{d-3}) = 1.
\end{eqnarray*}
nodes.section: 4 Irreducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement_short: Show $s_{d,n}$, hence $r_{d,n}$, is monic.

nodes.name: Reduce to s_{d,n}
nodes.statement: It suffices to show that this is true for $s_{d,n}(x)$.
nodes.section: 4 Irreducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to $s_{d,n}$.

nodes.name: Leading coefficient computation
nodes.statement:
Since the leading coefficient of $p_{d,n} (x)$ is $F_d n + F_{d-2}$,
we deduce that the leading coefficient of $s_{d,n}(x)$ is equal to
\begin{eqnarray*}
& (-1)^{d-1} (F_{d-1}(F_d n + F_{d-2})-F_d(F_{d-1}n + F_{d-3})) \\ 
& =
(-1)^{d-1}(F_{d-1}F_{d-2}-F_dF_{d-3}) = 1.
\end{eqnarray*}
nodes.section: 4 Irreducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement_short: Fibonacci identity gives leading coefficient 1.

nodes.name: Value of r_{d,n} at x_n
nodes.section: 4 Irreducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 3

nodes.name: Degree of r_{d,n}
nodes.statement: Observe that the degree of the polynomial $r_{d,n} (x)$ is $d$.
nodes.section: 4 Irreducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement_short: $\deg r_{d,n}=d$.

nodes.name: Claim (6): close conjugate roots
nodes.statement:
We claim that
$r_{d,n} (x)$ has two complex conjugate roots $v_{d,n}$ and
$\overline{v_{d,n}}$ close to $x_n $,
more precisely they are equal to
$$
\eqalign{
1/n-1/n^2+2/n^3- & 5/n^4+13/n^5- \ldots + \cr
& + (-1)^d F_{2d-5}/n^{d-1} \pm i/n^{(2d-1)/2} + O(1/n^{d}). \cr} \eqno (6)
$$
Indeed, the polynomials $F_d^2 p_{d,n}^2(x)$ and $F_{d-1}^2 x p_{d-1,n}^2(x)$
have double 
roots $y_{d+1,n}$ and $y_{d,n}$, resp., in the disc 
$|x-x_n|\leq 1/n^{2d+1}$,
resp. $|x-x_n|\leq 1/n^{2d-1}$.
Moreover, we have $F_d^2 p_{d,n}^2(x) < xs_{d,n}^2(x)$ when 
$|x-x_n| = 1/n^{2d+1}$
and $F_{d-1}^2 x p_{d-1,n}^2(x) < s_{d,n}^2(x)$ when 
$|x-x_n| = 1/n^{2d-1}$.
Hence, by Rouch\'e's theorem, the polynomial
$r_{d,n} (x)$ has two roots $v$ satisfying $|v-x_n |<1/n^{d-1}$.
Using a complex version of Taylor's theorem,
by writing the roots $v$ of $r_{d,n} (x)$ close to $x_n$
as $v =x_n +\beta+\gamma i$ with $\gamma > 0$, we get 
$$
\eqalign{
0 & =r_{d,n}(x_n +\beta+\gamma i) \cr
& = r_{d,n}(x_n ) + (\beta+\gamma i)r'_{d,n}(x_n )+
(\beta+\gamma i)^2r''_{d,n}(x_n )/2+ O(1/n^{3d-5}). \cr}
$$
Note that we have
$$
r'_{2d+1,n}(x_n ) =\frac{2F_dF_{d+1}}{n^{2d-1}} + O(1/n^{2d}),
$$
$$
r'_{2d,n}(x_n ) =\frac{2F_{d-1}F_{d-2}}{n^{2d-2}} + O(1/n^{2d-1}),
$$
and
$$
r''_{d,n}(x_n ) = 2F_{\lfloor (d-1)/2 \rfloor}^2 n^2 + O(n).
$$
By considering imaginary parts in the above Taylor's formula we get
\begin{eqnarray*}
\beta &=& - \frac{r'_{d,n}(x_n)}{r''_{d,n}(x_n)} + O(\gamma^{-1}r''_{d,n}(x_n)^{-1}n^{-3d+5}) \\
 &=& - \frac{F_{\lfloor (d-1)/2 \rfloor + (-1)^d}}{n^d} + O\left(\frac{1}{n^{d+1}}\right) +
O\left(\frac{1}{\gamma n^{3d-3}}\right).
\end{eqnarray*}
Since the distance between the roots $x_n +\beta+\gamma i$ and  
$x_n +\beta-\gamma i$ of $r_{d,n} (x)$ is equal to $2 \gamma$  
and $H(r_{d,n})=O(n^2)$, 
it follows from Mahler's theorem \cite{Mah64} quoted in the introduction that 
$\gamma \gg 1/n^{2d-2}$. Thus, $\beta = O(1/n^{d-1})$.
Moreover, $\beta = O(1/n^d)$, unless $\gamma \ll 1/n^{2d-3}$.
Looking at real parts leads to
$$
\eqalign{
\frac{F_{\lfloor (d-1)/2 \rfloor}^2}{n^{2d-3}} +
\frac{2\beta F_{\lfloor (d-1)/2 \rfloor}F_{\lfloor (d-1)/2 \rfloor
+ (-1)^d}}{n^{d-2}} + (\beta^2 - \gamma^2) &
F_{\lfloor (d-1)/2 \rfloor}^2 n^2 \cr
& = O\left(\frac{1}{n^{2d-2}}\right).}  \eqno{(7)}
$$
The assumption that $\gamma \ll 1/n^{2d-3}$ leads to a contradiction, 
by considering (7) as a quadratic equation
in $\beta$. Hence, we have $\beta = O(1/n^{d})$. Now (7) gives
$\gamma^2 = 1/n^{2d-1} + O(1/n^{2d})$, i.e.,
$\gamma = 1/n^{(2d-1)/2} + O(1/n^d)$, as claimed in (6).
nodes.section: 4 Irreducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement_short: Locate two complex conjugate roots of $r_{d,n}$ near $x_n$ via Rouche and Taylor expansion.

nodes.name: Double roots of the summands
nodes.statement:
Indeed, the polynomials $F_d^2 p_{d,n}^2(x)$ and $F_{d-1}^2 x p_{d-1,n}^2(x)$
have double 
roots $y_{d+1,n}$ and $y_{d,n}$, resp., in the disc 
$|x-x_n|\leq 1/n^{2d+1}$,
resp. $|x-x_n|\leq 1/n^{2d-1}$.
nodes.section: 4 Irreducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement_short: Summands have double roots very near $x_n$.

nodes.name: Rouche's theorem
nodes.statement:
Moreover, we have $F_d^2 p_{d,n}^2(x) < xs_{d,n}^2(x)$ when 
$|x-x_n| = 1/n^{2d+1}$
and $F_{d-1}^2 x p_{d-1,n}^2(x) < s_{d,n}^2(x)$ when 
$|x-x_n| = 1/n^{2d-1}$.
Hence, by Rouch\'e's theorem, the polynomial
$r_{d,n} (x)$ has two roots $v$ satisfying $|v-x_n |<1/n^{d-1}$.
nodes.section: 4 Irreducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement_short: Rouche gives two roots within $n^{-(d-1)}$ of $x_n$.

nodes.name: Taylor expansion
nodes.statement:
Using a complex version of Taylor's theorem,
by writing the roots $v$ of $r_{d,n} (x)$ close to $x_n$
as $v =x_n +\beta+\gamma i$ with $\gamma > 0$, we get 
$$
\eqalign{
0 & =r_{d,n}(x_n +\beta+\gamma i) \cr
& = r_{d,n}(x_n ) + (\beta+\gamma i)r'_{d,n}(x_n )+
(\beta+\gamma i)^2r''_{d,n}(x_n )/2+ O(1/n^{3d-5}). \cr}
$$
nodes.section: 4 Irreducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement_short: Expand $r_{d,n}$ at $x_n$ to second order.

nodes.name: Derivatives at x_n
nodes.section: 4 Irreducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement_short: Asymptotics of $r'$ and $r''$ at $x_n$.

nodes.name: Imaginary parts
nodes.section: 4 Irreducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement_short: Imaginary parts give $\beta$ in terms of $\gamma$.

nodes.name: Apply Mahler's bound
nodes.statement:
Since the distance between the roots $x_n +\beta+\gamma i$ and  
$x_n +\beta-\gamma i$ of $r_{d,n} (x)$ is equal to $2 \gamma$  
and $H(r_{d,n})=O(n^2)$, 
it follows from Mahler's theorem \cite{Mah64} quoted in the introduction that 
$\gamma \gg 1/n^{2d-2}$. Thus, $\beta = O(1/n^{d-1})$.
Moreover, $\beta = O(1/n^d)$, unless $\gamma \ll 1/n^{2d-3}$.
nodes.section: 4 Irreducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement_short: Mahler's theorem gives $\gamma\gg n^{-(2d-2)}$, hence bounds on $\beta$.

nodes.name: Real parts: (7)
nodes.statement:
Looking at real parts leads to
$$
\eqalign{
\frac{F_{\lfloor (d-1)/2 \rfloor}^2}{n^{2d-3}} +
\frac{2\beta F_{\lfloor (d-1)/2 \rfloor}F_{\lfloor (d-1)/2 \rfloor
+ (-1)^d}}{n^{d-2}} + (\beta^2 - \gamma^2) &
F_{\lfloor (d-1)/2 \rfloor}^2 n^2 \cr
& = O\left(\frac{1}{n^{2d-2}}\right).}  \eqno{(7)}
$$
nodes.section: 4 Irreducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement_short: Real parts give relation (7).

nodes.name: Exclude small gamma
nodes.statement:
The assumption that $\gamma \ll 1/n^{2d-3}$ leads to a contradiction, 
by considering (7) as a quadratic equation
in $\beta$. Hence, we have $\beta = O(1/n^{d})$.
nodes.section: 4 Irreducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement_short: Small $\gamma$ contradicts (7), so $\beta=O(n^{-d})$.

nodes.name: Determine gamma
nodes.statement:
Now (7) gives
$\gamma^2 = 1/n^{2d-1} + O(1/n^{2d})$, i.e.,
$\gamma = 1/n^{(2d-1)/2} + O(1/n^d)$, as claimed in (6).
nodes.section: 4 Irreducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 3

nodes.name: Irreducible factor R_{d,n}
nodes.statement:
Let $R_{d,n}(x)$ be the irreducible factor of $r_{d,n}(x)$ having roots
$v_{d,n}$ and $\overline{v_{d,n}}$. Denote by $\delta$ its degree.
Note that, since $H(r_{d,n})=O(n^2)$, Gelfond's inequality implies that
$$
H(R_{d,n})=O(n^2).    \eqno (8)
$$
nodes.section: 4 Irreducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement_short: Let $R_{d,n}$ be the irreducible factor with the close roots; Gelfond gives $H(R_{d,n})=O(n^2)$.

nodes.name: Resultant is nonzero
nodes.statement:
Denote by ${\rm Res}_{d,n}$ the resultant of
the polynomials $R_{d,n} (x)$ and $L_n(x)$.
Since ${\rm Res}_{d,n}$ is a rational integer and $x_n$ is not a root of $R_{d,n} (x)$, we have
$$
|{\rm Res}_{d,n}| \ge 1.   \eqno (9)
$$
nodes.section: 4 Irreducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement_short: The resultant of $R_{d,n}$ and $L_n$ is a nonzero integer.

nodes.name: Upper bound from resultant definition
nodes.statement:
Furthermore, the definition of the resultant of two polynomials (see e.g. \cite[p. 223]{BuLiv})
implies that (recall that $R_{d,n}(x)$ is monic)
$$
|{\rm Res}_{d,n}| \le  (n^2 + 3n+1)^{\delta} \prod_{t : R_{d,n} (t) = 0} \, |t - x_n|.
$$
nodes.section: 4 Irreducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement_short: Bound the resultant by a product over roots.

nodes.name: Bound using (6) and (8)
nodes.statement:
Since the product of the absolute values of all the roots of $R_{d,n} (x)$
different from $v_{d,n}$ and $\overline{v_{d,n}}$ is bounded
from above by $\sqrt{d+1}$ times
the height of $R_{d,n} (x)$ (see \cite[Exercise A.1]{BuLiv}), we deduce from (6) and (8) that
$$
|{\rm Res}_{d,n}| \ll n^{2 \delta} n^{-2d+1} n^2.
$$
nodes.section: 4 Irreducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement_short: $|{\rm Res}|\ll n^{2\delta-2d+3}$.

nodes.name: Degree of R_{d,n}
nodes.statement:
Combined with (9), this gives $2 \delta \ge 2d - 3$, thus
$$
\delta \in  \{d, d-1\}.
$$
This implies that either $r_{d,n}(x)$ is irreducible, or it has an integer
root (recall that any rational root of a monic polynomial must be a rational
integer).
nodes.section: 4 Irreducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement_short: $\delta\in\{d,d-1\}$, so $r_{d,n}$ is irreducible or has an integer root.

nodes.name: Possible integer roots
nodes.statement:
Assume that $r_{d,n}(x)$ is reducible, i.e., that it has an integer root.
This integer must divide $r_{d,n}(0)=F_{\lfloor (d-1)/2 \rfloor}^2$,
and, by (5),
it is of the form $-\alpha^2$ for an integer $\alpha$ dividing $F_{\lfloor (d-1)/2 \rfloor}$.
So, for any given degree $d$, there are only finitely many possibilities for the integer root
of $r_{d,n}(x)$.
nodes.section: 4 Irreducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement_short: An integer root must be $-\alpha^2$ with $\alpha\mid F_{\lfloor(d-1)/2\rfloor}$: finitely many options.

nodes.name: Write r_{d,n} as quadratic in n
nodes.statement:
Write $r_{d,n}(x)$ as
$$
r_{d,n}(x)=A_d(x)n^2+B_d(x)n+C_d(x).
$$
nodes.section: 4 Irreducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement_short: View $r_{d,n}$ as a quadratic in $n$.

nodes.name: Discriminant in n
nodes.statement:
By the definition of $r_{d,n}(x)$ and (1), it follows easily by induction
that the discriminant $B_d(x)^2 - 4A_d(x)C_d(x)$ of $r_{d,n}(x)$ with respect to $n$
is equal to $-4 F_{\lfloor (d-1)/2 \rfloor}^4 x^{2d-1}$.
In particular, this discriminant is nonzero at $x=-\alpha^2$,
and thus at least one of the numbers $A_d(-\alpha^2)$, $B_d(-\alpha^2)$, $C_d(-\alpha^2)$
is nonzero.
This shows that $r_{d,n}(x)$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Z}[n,x]$.
nodes.section: 4 Irreducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement_short: Discriminant in $n$ is $-4F^4x^{2d-1}\neq0$ at $x=-\alpha^2$.

nodes.name: No integer roots for large n
nodes.statement:
Furthermore, for given $\alpha$ there are exactly two (rational) values of $n$
such that $-\alpha^2$ is a root of $r_{d,n}(x)$. Hence, for sufficiently large
positive integer $n$, the polynomial $r_{d,n}(x)$ has no integer roots,
and therefore it is irreducible over $\mathbb{Z}[x]$.
nodes.section: 4 Irreducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement_short: Each $-\alpha^2$ is a root for only two values of $n$, so $r_{d,n}$ is irreducible for large $n$.

nodes.name: Conclude Theorem 3
nodes.statement:
Since
$$
{\rm sep}(r_{d,n}) = O(n^{-(d-1/2)}),
$$
we obtain
$$
e_{{\rm irr}}^* (d) \geq \frac{2d-1}{4},
$$
which proves Theorem \ref{tm3}.
\null \hfill \rule{2mm}{2mm}
nodes.section: 4 Irreducible monic polynomials: Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement_short: sep$(r_{d,n})=O(n^{-(d-1/2)})$ with height $O(n^2)$ gives $e^*_{\rm irr}(d)\ge(2d-1)/4$.

nodes.name: Product polynomial with a cluster
nodes.statement:
Let $\delta \ge 2$ and $h \ge 0$ be integers. The polynomial
$$
{\tilde P}_{\delta, h, n} (x) :=
P_{\delta, n} (x) \times p_{\delta,n} (x) \times \cdots \times p_{\delta+h, n} (x)
$$
has degree $(h+2)\delta + h(h+1)/2$, height $\ll  n^{h+4}$, and
it has a cluster of $h+3$ roots close
to each other.
nodes.section: 5 Clusters of roots
nodes.statement_short: $\tilde P_{\delta,h,n}$ has degree $(h+2)\delta+h(h+1)/2$, height $\ll n^{h+4}$ and a cluster of $h+3$ close roots.

nodes.name: Derive (12)
nodes.statement:
Setting $k = h+3$, a short calculation gives (12), since one can
multiply ${\tilde P}_{\delta, h, n} (x)$ by a suitable power of the monomial $x$.
nodes.section: 5 Clusters of roots
nodes.statement_short: With $k=h+3$, padding by powers of $x$ gives (12).

nodes.name: Monic case (13)
nodes.statement:
To get (13), it suffices, for $\delta$ even, to consider the polynomial
$$
{\tilde Q}_{\delta, h, n} (x) :=
Q_{\delta, n} (x) \times q_{\delta,n} (x) \times \cdots \times q_{\delta + 2 h, n} (x),
$$
multiplied by a suitable power of the monomial $x$.
We omit the details.
\null \hfill \rule{2mm}{2mm}
nodes.section: 5 Clusters of roots
nodes.statement_short: Use $\tilde Q_{\delta,h,n}$ built from $Q$ and $q$'s for (13); details omitted.
